title: Agent-DLC Method and Launchpad Architecture
html:
Goal: understand the five quality dimensions and six phases of Agent-DLC, and which Launchpad and AgentCore capability backs each one.

Five quality dimensions

Turn "is this agent any good?" from opinion into measurable criteria:

Dimension Question Typical metrics
🧠 Cognition Does it understand the business? Accuracy, tool-selection accuracy
✅ Quality Are the answers reliable? Faithfulness, helpfulness, ground-truth correctness
🛡️ Responsibility Is it safe and compliant? Harmful content, privacy leaks, unauthorized promises
💰 Cost What does it cost? Tokens per session, cost per invocation
⚡ Performance Can it handle the load? Latency, error rate

Six phases

Define → Build → Evaluate → Release → Observe → Improve. It is a flywheel, not a one-off pipeline: launch is not the finish line, and real production issues feed back into the criteria so the next round is stronger.

Stage What it does
1 Define Turns business goals into five-dimension criteria and a golden test set
2 Build Prompt, tools, retrieval and memory: a runnable agent
3 Evaluate Scores against the golden standard, attributed at session, trajectory and step level
4 Release A version reaches production only through the release gate, signed by someone other than its author
5 Observe Samples production traffic for online scoring and watches for silent drift
6 Improve Production failures join the set, so the golden standard keeps getting harder

All six stages turn around one golden standard (the golden test set plus the five-dimension criteria): Define produces it, Build follows it, Evaluate draws on it, Release decides by it, Observe reuses it, and Improve feeds production failures back into it.

The console organises these six phases as a storyline: the journey strip at the top of a page shows which phase you are in, a "next step" card appears after each step you finish, and the "Your turn" panel on the home page lists what the current account has to do. Follow it and you will not miss a step someone else has to sign.

Met a word you do not know? Terms with a dotted underline in the console open their definition when clicked; press ⌘K (Ctrl+K on Windows) to search terms, or open "Glossary" from the help menu at the top right. An Agent-DLC term card also lists the storyline steps that use it.

Four things the platform holds for you

Traditionally, "can this ship?" is settled in a review meeting. Launchpad's Agent-DLC module splits that decision into four platform-owned, auditable objects:

Object Question Key rules
Criteria set What counts as good? Versioned; every dimension has a criterion or an explicit not-applicable note; at least one red line; a red line cannot be decided by an LLM judge; once published, it is signed by someone other than its author
Golden set What is the evidence? Three splits: dev / regression / holdout; the holdout is written only by a one-time stratified seed and sealed afterwards
Judge calibration May an LLM judge stand in for a person? At least two blind human annotators, Cohen's κ; a non-annotator decides whether the judge is aligned; an unaligned judge only observes and cannot block a release
Gate Can this version ship? Fixed order: red lines (any violation → BLOCKED, never waivable) → denominator (more than 5% undetermined → INVALID) → per-dimension thresholds (a miss can be waived) → observed criteria

INVALID is not a failure: it means the evidence cannot decide — for example, the criteria are unsigned or the holdout was never run.

Gated release: a gate in front of traffic

Once the workspace release policy is gated and release-ops has moved the agent onto named endpoints, it serves through two of them (a new agent stays on the default endpoint until then, and its deploys take effect directly):

flowchart LR
  Dev[developer redeploys] --> C[candidate endpoint]
  C --> G{Gate evaluation<br/>regression + holdout}
  G -- PASS --> S[release-ops signs]
  S --> L[live endpoint]
  G -- BLOCKED --> W[Request waiver / fix]
  L -. rollback .-> P[previous version]
  • A deploy only updates candidate; live, which carries production traffic, is untouched.
  • Only after sign-off (signer ≠ requester) does live point at the new version; rollback points live back at the previous one and deletes nothing.
  • Every invoke path — console chat, public API (/v1/...) — uses the live endpoint.

Launchpad architecture at a glance

  • Several creation methods, one deploy pipeline: managed Harness (no code), Strands Agents (form or visual canvas), other agent SDK containers, and BYOC (bring your own code) all converge on the five stages generate → package → provision → deploy → register.
  • One invoke chain: the console chat and the public API (/v1/...) share a single invoke entry point, so they behave identically.
  • AWS is the source of truth: the local database keeps only identifiers and derived progress; runtime status, traces and evaluation results are always read back from AWS.
  • Private network by default: an administrator registers network profiles and storage entries up front, so a participant creating an agent just picks a template and never deals with VPCs, subnets or mounts. This environment comes with the network profile workshop-private and the S3 Files storage workshop-files already registered.
  • Multi-user, permission-based: there are four global roles — admin, organization steward (manages accounts and the organization structure, never sees project data), operator and member. Inside a project, members split the work by project role template: project owner, developer, business owner, release ops, subject-matter expert, tool steward, viewer. Permissions such as signing criteria, admitting samples and deciding calibration are granted to named people, never by role; separation of duties is checked by account — the requester and the signer must be different accounts. Every decision is written to the audit log.

Organization: departments, project groups, projects

Agents, criteria sets, golden sets, evaluations and API keys all belong to a project. Projects can be organised under departments and project groups, so access is granted per team and cost is rolled up:

Level Example in this workshop Purpose
Department 客服中心 (Customer Service) Organizational dimension, rolls up its projects
Project group 零售与电商 (Retail & E-commerce), 旅行 OTA (Travel OTA) A set of related projects, granted together
Project retail-service, travel-service Boundary of resources and members: projects cannot see each other by default

The flywheel main line runs in retail-service; travel-service shows project isolation and is used in the team lab.

Chapter map

The participant chapters come in three groups, and this chapter belongs to the first one; an appendix for the organiser comes after them.

Group Chapter Content Main accounts
